title: Playing in Naples
excerpt: Naples street night life was epic
body:
# Playing in Naples

I've run through a lot of cities on foot—sometimes literally, sometimes just wandering—but nothing quite prepared me for the sensory overload that is Naples at night. And I mean that as a compliment, though my sleep schedule and wallet might disagree.

There's this thing that happens when you step into the old town after sunset. The narrow streets, which during the day feel like historic monuments you're supposed to respectfully admire, suddenly transform into something alive. Not just alive—*feral* in the best possible way. People spill out of cafés and restaurants onto the cobblestones. Scooters weave through pedestrians with the kind of casual disregard for traffic laws that would get you arrested in most places. And the energy? It's infectious.

I found myself wandering aimlessly through those winding streets like I was the main character in some Italian film I had no business starring in. Every corner turned revealed something new: a restaurant with waiters aggressively welcoming you inside, a tiny bar packed shoulder-to-shoulder with locals drinking espresso like it's going out of style, a street vendor selling literally anything you could want—and probably some things you didn't know you wanted until you saw them.

The food was the real revelation. I'm not talking about some precious, Instagram-worthy plating situation. I'm talking about *eating*. Grabbing a pizza from a corner joint that looked like it hadn't been renovated since 1987 and somehow serving the best pizza you've ever had. Street vendors handing you fresh seafood. Pasta that made me question every meal I'd eaten before Naples. The city isn't trying to impress you with culinary pretension—it's just feeding you like it actually cares whether you eat well. Which, apparently, Neapolitans do.

What struck me most was how the entire city seemed to be *playing*. Not in a touristy, performative way, but genuinely having a good time. Families, couples, groups of friends—everyone was out there, loud and happy and taking their sweet time about it. The pace is deliberate. Nobody's rushing to the next thing. You're supposed to linger, to engage, to argue passionately about soccer or politics or whatever random topic comes up.

I spent hours just moving through the streets with no particular destination, eating when hungry, stopping to watch street musicians, getting temporarily lost and somehow always finding something better than what I was originally looking for. 

If you're an ultrarunner like me, you spend a lot of time alone in your own head on long trails. Naples is the antidote to that. It's loud and chaotic and full of strangers who somehow make you feel less like a stranger. You don't need a training plan or gear list—just the willingness to get a little lost and say yes to whatever comes next.

Highly recommend. Your feet and your diet will hate you, but your soul will thank you.

title: Spoiling the Boys
excerpt: Having fun with my boys. Look at that bone!
body:
# Spoiling the Boys

There's something uniquely satisfying about watching your dogs lose their minds over a toy. Not in that frantic, neurotic way—I mean the pure, unadulterated joy that comes from a really good find. And when you're the one who brought home the goods? Well, that's when you get to feel like the best human in the world for approximately forty-seven seconds, until they move on to destroying the couch.

My Weimaraners, Apollo and Rocky, have very different ideas about what constitutes a good time. That's part of what makes watching them play so entertaining. Apollo is convinced he's a parrot. I'm not sure how else to explain it. The moment I sit down, this seventy-pound gray missile of a dog decides my shoulder is his perch. He'll hop up there, settle in like he owns the place, and just... hang out. It's equal parts adorable and ridiculous, especially when he realizes he's too big for this whole "lap dog" concept but commits to the bit anyway. There's nothing quite like having a Weimaraner on your shoulder, looking absolutely convinced that this is exactly where he belongs.

Rocky, on the other hand, has evolved into something of a self-entertainer. He's the guy who steals a stuffed animal, carries it to the yard, and then throws it for himself. I watch this happening and can't help but laugh at the absurdity of it. He's basically playing fetch... with himself. There's a confidence in it, too—like he's figured out a loophole in the game and isn't waiting around for a human to participate.

But both of them? They lose it completely over this dinosaur bone I picked up recently. We're talking full-body wiggle, tail at helicopter speeds, completely unhinged dedication to this thing. It's enormous—easily bigger than both their heads—and somehow it's the most captivating object ever to enter their universe. They take turns with it, gnaw on it, carry it around like it's the Holy Grail. I keep waiting for one of them to destroy it, but so far, it's holding up better than I expected.

These moments remind me why I love these goofballs so much. The unconditional enthusiasm, the weird little quirks that make each of them distinct—it's genuinely one of the highlights of my day. Apollo doing his awkward shoulder impression, Rocky throwing toys at himself, both of them absolutely mesmerized by an oversized dinosaur bone.

Yeah, I'm definitely spoiling them. And I'd do it again in a heartbeat.

title: Amalfi Coast
excerpt: A cold beverage after a warm hike.
body:
# A Week of Absolute Indulgence on the Amalfi Coast

Look, I'm going to be straight with you: I'm a guy who spends most of his time covered in sweat and dirt, pushing his body to breaking points in the mountains. So when Donna suggested a week-long sailing adventure on the Amalfi coast, my first instinct was to find an ultramarathon to talk her out of it. But she gave me that look—you know the one—and here we are. And I'm absolutely not complaining.

We boarded the *Dream Yachts* catamaran with four other adventurers and promptly handed our lives over to our skipper, who actually knew what he was doing. Unlike me with a sailboat. I can navigate mountains blind, but ask me to trim a jib and I'm useless. The beauty of this setup? We didn't have to be useful. We just had to show up, breathe in the Mediterranean air, and let someone else do the heavy lifting for once.

The catamaran became our floating basecamp—a weird concept for someone whose basecamp usually involves a sleeping bag and the faint smell of regret. But this one came with a chef. An actual chef. Who prepared meals so good I stopped questioning my life choices around day two.

The highlights blurred together in the best way possible. We hiked the Path of Gods, that legendary trek along the Amalfi cliffside where you're basically walking along vertigo itself. The views are ridiculous—the kind that make you understand why humans have spent thousands of years writing poetry about this coast. My legs barely remembered they were legs by that point, which was somehow comforting. This I understood.

Capri was impossibly blue and absurdly crowded, but there's something about sailing into those grottos and seeing the Blue Grotto for real that cuts through the tourist nonsense. Naples deserved more time than we gave it—I could taste the history in the air, feel the chaos in the narrow streets. That's a place that demands you slow down and actually pay attention.

But here's what I didn't expect: the simple peace of being on the water. No race clock. No summit waiting. Just the gentle rock of the boat, decent wine, good conversation, and my wife beside me. The chef would deliver another meal. Someone would point out a pod of dolphins. The skipper would adjust course for some new adventure, and we'd just... go.

I'm already looking at calendars, pretending I'm thinking about my next 100-miler. But I'm really just counting down to when we can do this again. Sometimes the best adventures aren't about testing your limits—they're about expanding them in directions you didn't expect.
